$comment: Credential-broker provider catalogue — a RUNTIME-IMMUTABLE, read-only file shipped with OpenRegister. It defines the external providers the broker may call, host-locked, and the constrained-proxy allow-rules (permitted method + path-prefix patterns) that bound what any credential can ever do. These allow-rules are a security control: they MUST NOT be widenable at runtime via any API — new providers/rules ship in a reviewed release only (design.md D2, ADR-031 exception). The broker reads this file server-side; it is NOT an OpenRegister schema, NOT register-seeded objects, and has no create/update/delete endpoint. '{secret}' in an authScheme.template is substituted by the broker with the vault-held token at call time; the token itself never appears here. Doffin caveat: the baseUrl is Doffin's Azure-APIM-hosted Public API on its BETA host, and the GET /notices rule is carried from the spectr Norway connector contract (not live-verifiable without a real subscription key, 2026-07-06); if the path or host moves, the broker fails closed (403) and the fix is another reviewed release of this file.
$fleetComment: 2026-07-12 — the catalogue held only github/gitlab/doffin, and CredentialController::create() rejects an unknown provider. So Mollie, Stripe, Adyen, CCV, KVK, Twilio, MessageBird, CM.com and the LLM providers could not be brokered AT ALL — you could not even create a credential for them. Every app therefore kept custody of its own secrets, not out of carelessness but because compliance was impossible. This release adds the providers whose auth the broker can actually express: ONE request header carrying ONE secret (injectAuth() substitutes {secret} into a single header template — it cannot do a token exchange, mTLS, or a signing operation). Rules are scoped to the endpoints the fleet actually calls, taken from the adapters themselves — no root wildcards, no DELETE. STILL NOT BROKERABLE, each needing broker capability work rather than a catalogue entry: (1) BRP/HaalCentraal — OAuth2 client_credentials needs a token EXCHANGE (POST secret -> access_token -> call), which a static header template cannot do; (2) procest StUF — an mTLS client certificate rides the TLS handshake, not a header; (3) scholiq's tenant RSA key — needs a SIGN operation, it is never sent as a request header; (4) softwarecatalog's SMTP password and its SendGrid/Mailgun/Postmark/Mailjet keys — Symfony Mailer takes them in a transport DSN, and SMTP is not HTTP at all, so a constrained HTTP proxy cannot carry them (these move to Doriath custody with the app holding only a credentialRef). Self-hosted targets (xWiki, and OpenConnector's arbitrary Sources) cannot be host-locked from an immutable file at all — they need a per-install, admin-approved provider registration, which is a broker design change.
$injectOnlyComment: 2026-07-14 (v1.4.0) — the last paragraph above named the standing gap: OpenConnector's arbitrary/self-hosted Sources cannot be host-locked from an immutable file, so their secrets never had a compliant home and stayed embedded in the source schema (ocon#147). The `inject_only` providers below close that gap WITHOUT weakening the host-locked proxy. They carry NO baseUrl and NO allowRules, so the broker's request() proxy path REFUSES them (CredentialBrokerService::request() denies an inject_only provider — an unbounded host is exactly what must never be proxied). They are reachable ONLY through CredentialBrokerService::resolveInjectable(), which runs guards 1+2 (owner + allowedApps) and hands the raw secret to the SAME-INSTANCE calling app, which injects it itself against whatever host its own config names. The trade-off is deliberate and narrow: the secret leaves OR into the trusted in-process app (NOT zero-knowledge, unlike the SaaS proxy above), but it lives in Doriath and the app's schema holds only a credentialRef — which is the whole point (never store a secret in a schema; store a reference). The five entries mirror OpenConnector's Source `auth` schemes; the app decides how to inject per its own Source.auth, so the authScheme here is descriptive only. 2026-07-16 (v1.6.0) — `inject_only` is NO LONGER only the five generic-* entries: `anthropic-cli` (grouped with the other anthropic providers above, not here) is inject_only for a different reason. It is not an unbounded host — it is a CLI. A vendor CLI needs its token in the process ENVIRONMENT, so there is no outbound request to proxy and no header to substitute, and the constrained-proxy path cannot express it at any host. Read `inject_only` as 'the broker cannot bound this call, so it refuses to make it and the guarded resolveInjectable() path applies instead' — which covers BOTH an unbounded host and a non-HTTP consumer. When adding a provider, prefer a host-locked proxy entry; reach for inject_only only when the broker genuinely cannot make the call itself.
$oauth2Comment: 2026-09-04 (v1.9.0) — the $fleetComment above says the broker "cannot do a token exchange", and named that as the reason BRP/HaalCentraal and every OAuth2 provider were unbrokerable. FOR THE `oauth2-token-set` KIND, THAT IS NO LONGER TRUE. An entry declaring `kind: "oauth2-token-set"` carries an `oauth2` block naming its authorization, token and revoke endpoints, its refresh grant, its client authentication method and whether it takes PKCE; the broker stores a whole token set as ONE opaque secret in the custody leaf, refreshes it on read past a margin and on a daily sweep, rotates it atomically under a per-credential lock, and injects only the access token. The rest of the sentence still stands verbatim: mTLS, a signing operation, and an SMTP transport DSN remain unexpressible, and client_credentials is NOT covered here either — this kind is the AUTHORIZATION CODE grant with a refresh token, minted by a person consenting, which is a different shape from a machine-to-machine client_credentials exchange. An entry with NO `kind` is `secret` and behaves exactly as it always has; nothing existing moved. Two entries (mastodon, bluesky) declare `baseUrlFrom: "instanceBaseUrl"` instead of a fixed `baseUrl`, because their API host belongs to the connected ACCOUNT rather than to the provider. That MOVES the host-lock rather than removing it: the host is validated at mint (absolute https, registrable domain, never a loopback or private-range address), pinned onto the credential, and immutable afterwards, so each credential is locked to one host for its whole life while the allow-rules below still bound every call. Adding an OAuth2 provider is still a reviewed release of this file, and an endpoint supplied in a request body is ignored.

adyen-test.title: Adyen (test)
adyen-test.$comment: A separate entry, not a flag: baseUrl is the host-lock, so live and test cannot share one. The credentials differ anyway.

twilio.title: Twilio
twilio.$comment: Twilio is HTTP Basic (accountSid:authToken). The secret stored in the vault is the base64 of that pair, so the single-header template can carry it.

openai.title: OpenAI
openai.$comment: Host-locked to the public API. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on another host cannot be brokered through this entry — the broker fails closed (403), which is the intended behaviour for an immutable catalogue.

anthropic.title: Anthropic (Claude) — API key
anthropic.$comment: Host-locked to the public API. API-key auth: injected as the x-api-key header. Used by Hermiq's anthropic chat provider (authMode: api_key). An Anthropic-compatible endpoint on another host cannot be brokered through this entry — the broker fails closed (403).

anthropic-oauth.title: Anthropic (Claude Max) — OAuth subscription
anthropic-oauth.$comment: Host-locked to the public API. Claude Max/Pro subscription OAuth token: injected as the Authorization: Bearer header (Hermiq additionally sends the anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20 header, which is not a secret and passes through). PERSONAL-scope only per the Anthropic Terms of Service — a Max subscription is for that individual's own use; never share it across users.

anthropic-cli.title: Anthropic (Claude Max) — CLI subscription
anthropic-cli.$comment: inject_only: NO baseUrl, NO allowRules — request() denies it, exactly like the generic-* entries below. Resolved ONLY through resolveInjectable(), which runs guards 1+2 (owner + allowedApps) and hands the raw secret to the same-instance calling app. The secret is a Claude Max/Pro subscription OAuth token (from `claude setup-token`); Hermiq injects it into the hermiq-llm-runner ExApp's `claude` CLI process ENVIRONMENT as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. It is inject_only because a CLI needs the token in its env: there is no outbound request for the broker to proxy and no header to substitute, so the constrained-proxy path cannot express this at all. The trade-off is the same deliberate one the generic-* entries make: the secret LEAVES OpenRegister into the trusted in-process app (NOT zero-knowledge), bounded by those two guards, with Doriath holding custody and the app's config holding only a credentialRef. PERSONAL SCOPE ONLY per the Anthropic Terms of Service — a Max/Pro subscription is for that individual's own use; this credential MUST be rejected at organisation scope and may serve only its owner. Prefer the host-locked `anthropic` proxy entry (pay-per-token API key) wherever it works: it is zero-knowledge and strictly stronger. Do NOT use this entry for the direct Messages API — Anthropic refuses a subscription OAuth token there (HTTP 429 rate_limit_error carrying no rate-limit counters, verified 2026-07-16); the official CLI is the ToS-sanctioned path for a subscription. The authScheme below is DESCRIPTIVE ONLY — the broker injects nothing for this provider.

allowRules.$why: Finding queued work across an organisation in ONE call. hydra's sequencer runs on a schedule, and a schedule tick carries no repository — so it searches the org for the queue label and reads the repository back off whatever it finds. The alternative is enumerating the org and querying each repo in turn, which hydra's retired supervisor already tried: 41 repos x 5 label queries = 205 calls per tick, and the forge's abuse governor started 403'ing every request from that IP for ~15 minutes. This is read-only, host-locked to api.github.com like every rule here, and returns strictly less per issue than the GET /repos/* grant already present above. It is the issues counterpart of /search/repositories on the line above, which is already allowed.

Opening a pull request. Added so OpenBuild's export-to-GitHub can run through the broker instead of taking custody of the user's Personal Access Token: it pushes a tree (blobs/trees/commits/refs — already allowed) and then opens a PR, which was the ONE call the rules did not cover, and the only reason that path still held a raw PAT. Strictly less dangerous than the repo-write grants already present above (PUT /repos/*/contents/*, POST /repos/*/git/*), and it retires an app-held credential.

Bringing a pull request's branch up to date with its base. hydra-flows-first-port task 2.2 asked whether the PRE-MERGE step should resolve locally and land a fresh commit, or let the forge do it. DECIDED 2026-07-31: the forge does it, and this grant is what makes that possible. Resolving locally needs a working tree and the flow plane has none — the sidecar that runs an agent step is read_only, mounts nothing and holds no checkout, which is the same constraint that stops the builder and reviewer stages being agent steps at all. Letting GitHub perform the three-way merge server-side is the right division of labour: the forge owns merging, the flow owns deciding, and a conflict the forge cannot resolve comes back as a refusal rather than as a silently wrong tree. Narrower than it looks — it can only merge a pull request's OWN base into its OWN head, so it cannot move an arbitrary ref the way PATCH /repos/*/git/refs/* can.

Merging a pull request. PO decision 2026-07-31, and it makes an existing capability HONEST rather than adding a new one: PATCH /repos/*/git/refs/* (already granted above) can fast-forward a base branch to a PR head, which GitHub records as a merged PR. So the merge was always reachable — the rules just did not say so, and ConductionNL/openregister#2203 was filed on exactly that gap. A rule the catalogue forbids but a one-line call achieves is worse than an explicit grant, because it makes the allow-list unreliable as a statement of what a credential can do. Naming it here means merge authority is reviewable, greppable and revocable in one place, instead of being an emergent property of the refs rule. Whoever holds this credential can merge; scope it accordingly.

Adding a label to an issue. A label write is not decoration — it is how hydra's pipeline is COMMANDED (a label on an issue is the instruction to build, review, ship), so with nothing here matching issue labels the broker refused the one call the whole command plane rests on, even with a valid PAT (ConductionNL/openregister#2165). The grant is narrower than every repo-write rule already present: it touches issue METADATA, never a byte of code, and cannot reach outside /issues/.

Removing a label from an issue — the other half of the command above; a pipeline that can only ever add a label cannot express a state TRANSITION. This is the catalogue's first DELETE, and it is deliberate: v1.5.0's blanket 'no DELETE' was about never brokering the deletion of a repository, a release or file content, which this cannot do. It removes one named label from one issue, is fully reversible by the POST rule directly above, and destroys no content.

CREATING an issue. This is how hydra reports what its gates found, and a finding nobody can see is a gate that may as well not have run — without this the pipeline analyses a repository and then silently discards its own output. Measured: `no allow-rule matches POST /repos/*/issues` was the last thing standing between the flow port and deleting the 3,258-line shell orchestrator it replaces. It is the CREATE half of the three issue rules beside it: bounded to /issues, it writes issue metadata and never a byte of code, cannot reach a repository, a release or file content, and is reversible through the PATCH rule below (close the issue). Deliberately far narrower than the workflow-dispatch grant this catalogue briefly carried and reverted (openregister#2240, reverted by #2242) — that one let a credential EXECUTE arbitrary code in the repository; this one lets it file a bug report.

Editing an issue's own fields — state (open/closed), assignee, title, body. Same class of workflow automation as the two label rules above and needed by the same pipeline: closing the issue is how a completed run reports done. Bounded to /issues/, so no repo, release or content write is reachable through it.

github-push.title: GitHub — repository push (fine-grained, one repo, contents only)
github-push.$comment: inject_only: NO baseUrl, NO allowRules — request() denies it, exactly like anthropic-cli and the generic-* entries. It exists because `git push` needs a CREDENTIAL, not a proxied API call: git speaks the smart-HTTP pack protocol to the forge, so there is no single request for the broker to make on the caller's behalf and no header for it to substitute. The host-locked `github` proxy entry above therefore returns null from resolveInjectable() BY DESIGN, and that null is a ROUTING SIGNAL ('use request()') rather than a denial — but request() cannot express a push, so a pushing stage has had no compliant credential home at all. This entry is that home. The secret LEAVES OpenRegister into the trusted in-process caller (hermiq), which hands it to the llm-runner sidecar in the /stage payload; the sidecar puts it in the child ENVIRONMENT behind GIT_ASKPASS — never on argv, because the process table is world-readable, and never in a file that outlives the run. ⚠️ WHAT MUST BE STORED HERE, because this entry cannot enforce it and nothing downstream can either: a FINE-GRAINED personal access token (or a GitHub App installation token, which is better — it expires in an hour) scoped to ONE repository with 'Contents: Read and write' and NOTHING ELSE. Specifically NOT 'Workflows': a credential that can edit .github/workflows obtains code execution on the forge's runners and escapes every other control around it. Not a classic PAT — its `repo` scope is account-wide and carries workflow write. Not an org-admin token. Shortest expiry the forge offers. ASSERT the absence rather than assuming it: attempt PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/.github/workflows/probe.yml and require the refusal 'refusing to allow a Personal Access Token to create or update workflow ... without `workflows` scope'. A 201 means the token is wrong and MUST be revoked instead of stored. The compensating controls live where the credential is USED, not here: the hermiq sidecar refuses any push whose destination is not the one declared repository, whose branch is not feature/<issue>/*, or whose diff touches .github/workflows, a dependency manifest, or anything outside the issue's declared scope — and it withholds the credential from the process that reads repository content, so none of those rules depends on a model's compliance. The forge's own branch rulesets (pull_request required on main/development/beta, bypass OrganizationAdmin only) are the backstop if the sidecar is bypassed. Deliberately a SEPARATE entry rather than making `github` inject_only: that entry's whole value is that its secret never leaves OpenRegister, and flipping it would silently widen every existing github credential in the fleet. Two entries means the pushing credential is greppable, reviewable and revocable on its own.

allowRules.$why: GitLab's equivalent of the three GitHub issue rules above, in ONE rule because GitLab models it differently: there is no labels sub-resource — labels, state and assignee are all fields of the issue, mutated with `PUT /projects/:id/issues/:iid` (`add_labels` / `remove_labels` / `state_event` / `assignee_ids`). So the same workflow automation needs a single issue-update grant rather than a POST+DELETE pair. Bounded to /issues/; no repository, release or file write is reachable through it.

linkedin.title: LinkedIn (member and organisation posting)
linkedin.$comment: kind oauth2-token-set: the stored secret is a whole token set, not a bare string, and the broker refreshes it. Host-locked to the REST API. Scopes are requested at connect time; the Community Management API grants (w_organization_social, r_organization_social) require LinkedIn's Community Management application to be approved for the client, which is a filing, not a code change. LinkedIn does NOT support PKCE on the authorization code grant, so `pkce` is `none` — the connect flow still generates and holds a verifier, it is simply not sent.

allowRules.$why: Publishing a post as the connected member or organisation. This is the one write the marketing programme needs from LinkedIn.
Reading back a post the credential itself published, to record its permanent id and URL.
Reading likes and comments on the connected account's own posts.
Impression and engagement statistics for the connected organisation's own shares.
Follower counts for the connected organisation.
The connected member's own identity, used to fill the account handle and display name on the credential.

meta-graph.title: Meta Graph (Facebook Pages and Instagram Business)
meta-graph.$comment: kind oauth2-token-set. Meta has no refresh_token: a short-lived token is traded for a long-lived one with grant_type=fb_exchange_token against the same token endpoint, which is why `refreshGrant` names it. There is no revoke endpoint on the token host — revoking is DELETE /{user-id}/permissions, which is a Graph call rather than an OAuth2 one, so `revokeEndpoint` is null and disconnecting deletes locally. Personal Facebook and Instagram profiles cannot be posted to through the API at all; only Pages and Instagram Business accounts.

allowRules.$why: Publishing to a connected Page's feed.
Uploading an image that a Page post references.
Creating an Instagram Business media container, the first half of an Instagram publish.
Publishing a prepared Instagram media container, the second half.
Reading views, likes, comments and shares on the connected account's own posts. Reach and impressions were withdrawn by Meta in June 2026; the adapter normalises what remains.
Listing the Pages the connected user administers, so the connect flow can name the account the credential belongs to.

x.title: X (formerly Twitter)
x.$comment: kind oauth2-token-set. X requires PKCE with S256 and issues a refresh token only when offline.access is granted, so that scope is in the defaults; without it a connection lapses at the first expiry and needs a relink rather than a refresh. X is pay-per-use, so the consuming app is expected to hold a spend budget with a hard stop; the broker does not meter.

allowRules.$why: Publishing a post.
Reading back the connected account's own post, including its public metrics.
The connected account's own identity, used to fill the handle and display name on the credential.
The connected account's own timeline, used for the metrics pull.

mastodon.title: Mastodon (per-instance)
mastodon.$comment: kind oauth2-token-set with baseUrlFrom: Mastodon has no single API host, so the host comes from the credential's own instanceBaseUrl rather than from this file. That is a MOVE of the host-lock, not a removal: the host is validated once at mint (absolute https, registrable domain, never a loopback or private-range address), pinned onto the credential, and immutable afterwards, so a credential is locked to one server for its whole life. The allow-rules below still bound what any Mastodon credential can ever do, exactly as for a fixed-host entry. The oauth2 endpoints are paths, resolved against the same pinned host. Mastodon has no central application registry: the connect flow registers an application at the account's own server (POST /api/v1/apps), stores the client id as non-secret metadata and the client secret as a separate brokered credential. No relay is needed, because the tenant's own callback is registered at registration time.

allowRules.$why: Publishing a status.
Reading back the connected account's own status, including its reblog and favourite counts.
Uploading media a status references.
The connected account's own identity, used to fill the handle and display name on the credential.
Follower counts for the connected account.

bluesky.title: Bluesky (AT Protocol) — preview
bluesky.$comment: kind oauth2-token-set with baseUrlFrom, for the same reason as mastodon: the API host is the account's own PDS. AT Protocol OAuth needs no relay at all, because the client publishes its own metadata JSON and the instance serves that itself, so the tenant's Nextcloud is its own OAuth client. ⚠️ PREVIEW: AT Protocol requires DPoP-bound access tokens, and the DPoP proof layer is NOT implemented by the change that added this entry. A Bluesky connection can therefore be minted and refreshed but its access token will be refused by a PDS until DPoP lands. The entry ships anyway so the gap is visible in the catalogue rather than absent from it; the follow-up is credential-oauth2-bluesky-dpop. The authorization server is discovered per host rather than declared here.

allowRules.$why: Publishing a post as a repository record.
Reading back the connected account's own feed, which is where a post's like and repost counts are read.
The connected account's own profile, used to fill the handle and display name on the credential.
Follower counts for the connected account.

google-search-console.title: Google Search Console (read-only)
google-search-console.$comment: kind oauth2-token-set, host-locked to the Search Console API. A SEPARATE entry from google-analytics rather than one 'google' entry with two hosts, for exactly the reason the adyen live and test entries are separate: the baseUrl IS the host-lock, so two hosts cannot share one entry. Read-only scope only. ⚠️ A Google OAuth client left in testing status has its refresh tokens revoked after seven days; for a public-sector tenant the first-class path is a service account added as a property user, which skips the consent screen and this entry entirely.

allowRules.$why: The one query the keyword-intelligence work needs: clicks, impressions, CTR and position per query and page.
Listing the properties the connected account may read, so a tenant can pick one at connect time.

google-analytics.title: Google Analytics Data API (read-only)
google-analytics.$comment: kind oauth2-token-set, host-locked to the Analytics Data API. Separate from google-search-console because the host differs; the OAuth endpoints are Google's own and are shared. Read-only scope only. Matomo is the first-party alternative and is preferred for public-sector tenants, who commonly forbid third-party trackers outright.

allowRules.$why: Running a report against a property the connected account may read. Read-only by construction; the Data API has no write surface.

generic-apikey.title: Generic API key (app-injected)
generic-apikey.$comment: inject_only: no baseUrl, no allowRules. The broker will NOT proxy this — request() denies it. It is resolved app-side via resolveInjectable(): the calling app reads the raw key and injects it into its own request header against its own host. The secret is the bare API key.

generic-bearer.title: Generic bearer token (app-injected)
generic-bearer.$comment: inject_only. The secret is the bare token; the app injects `Authorization: Bearer {secret}` (or the equivalent for its Source.auth) against its own host.

generic-basic.title: Generic HTTP Basic password (app-injected)
generic-basic.$comment: inject_only. The secret is the PASSWORD only; the username is non-sensitive and stays readable on the app's own config. The app combines them into `Authorization: Basic base64(user:secret)`.

generic-oauth2.title: Generic OAuth2 client secret (app-injected)
generic-oauth2.$comment: inject_only. The secret is the OAuth2 client_secret; the non-sensitive client_id, token URL and scope stay on the app's own config. The app performs the token exchange itself (the broker cannot — a static header template cannot do a token exchange).

generic-jwt.title: Generic JWT signing secret (app-injected)
generic-jwt.$comment: inject_only. The secret is the JWT signing secret; the non-sensitive claims and algorithm stay on the app's own config. The app generates and signs the JWT itself (the broker cannot sign).
